name: Sooty
summary: The dark countershading that lies over a horse's topline, crest, shoulder and croup and makes it look darker than its base colour says - a muddy palomino, a smutty buckskin, a bay people keep calling black. It does nothing visible on a plain black. Held here as a dosage of two made-up alleles: no gene, locus, variant or DNA test for sooty has been published, so no position can be given. The name probably covers several things - black hairs mixed through the coat, dark-tipped hairs along the topline, and a general darkening of chestnut towards liver - and its control may differ between chestnut-based coats and coats with black points. It is heritable: in 1,369 foals of five Franches-Montagnes stallions (Henner et al. 2002) dark chestnut and dark bay looked recessive, in that breed only and with no variant found; a 2021 genome-wide study found a region containing SALL1 associated with how intense a chestnut is, a lead for chestnut darkening, not a sooty gene. It touches only the body coat, not build, speed or the long hair, and should not be confused with dun.

phenotypes.name: Wild type
phenotypes.description: No dark overlay - whatever the base colour and the dilutions made, that is what shows.

phenotypes.name: Faint sooty
phenotypes.description: A dark haze along the spine and a little shading over the croup. Easy to miss, and easy to mistake for a dun's dorsal stripe - which it is not: there are no leg bars, no shoulder bar and no mask with it.

phenotypes.name: Sooty
phenotypes.description: An obviously darker topline, crest and upper barrel over a clearer belly and flank - the countershading the word usually means.

phenotypes.name: Heavy sooty
phenotypes.description: A dark cape over the shoulder, back and croup, with the base colour left showing mostly low on the sides. On a chestnut-based coat the lower legs go muddy with it.

phenotypes.name: Extreme sooty
phenotypes.description: Dark over nearly the whole body. A bay reads as brown or black, a buckskin as a dark bay, and a palomino as a bronze horse - which is the commonest reason a coat cannot be identified from a photograph.
